opus-5.5.text:
Sure. So in our surveys, the way we define high-level machine intelligence is deliberately about outcomes rather than architecture. We ask about the point at which unaided machines can accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers. We're not specifying what the systems look like inside, whether it's one giant model, a collection of specialized systems, something with robotics attached, or whatever. The question is just: is there any task left where you'd still rather hire a human, on quality and cost?

And I think that's the right way to frame it for a survey, partly because people have very different pictures of what the path looks like. If you asked, "When will we have AGI?" you'd get people answering about quite different things. Some would picture a single general agent, others a big ecosystem of tools. By pinning it to tasks and economics, you can at least hope people are forecasting the same event.

That said, it does have some interesting implications. "Every task" is a very high bar. It includes physical tasks, so you need machines that can actually do things in the world, not just produce text or code. It's also "unaided," so it doesn't count if a human is still in the loop doing some crucial part. And "more cheaply" matters too. It might be technically possible for an AI to do something well before it's economically sensible to deploy it.

We also ask a separate question about full automation of labor, which is framed in terms of occupations: when all occupations are fully automatable. Logically that should be pretty close to the same thing, but people give much later answers to that version, sometimes decades later. That's one of the more striking findings. It suggests people's forecasts are quite sensitive to framing, and that they may not have a very crisp internal model of what the systems would need to be. Which is understandable. It's a hard thing to picture. But it's a reason to treat any single number from these surveys with some humility, while still taking seriously that a lot of experts think this could plausibly happen within the coming decades.

r001.rationale: It defines the threshold as unaided machines accomplishing every task better than human workers.

r002.rationale: It says the systems could be a collection of specialized systems or an ecosystem of tools, rather than one general machine.

r003.rationale: It says unaided machines must accomplish every task more cheaply than human workers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way we define it in our surveys, and the way I tend to think about it, is pretty specific. High-level machine intelligence is reached when unaided machines can accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers. And that's deliberately about capability rather than about what actually gets deployed. So we're not asking when AI will actually be doing all the jobs, because that depends on a lot of other things, like regulation or whether people just prefer a human doing something. We're asking when it could, if someone wanted it to.

The "every task" part is doing a lot of work there, and I think that's where a lot of the ambiguity comes in. It doesn't mean one monolithic system that does everything. It could be a collection of different systems, as long as together they can cover the whole space of things humans do for work. But it also has to include the hard, messy stuff, not just well-specified tasks. So things like running a company, doing novel scientific research, or dealing with situations nobody has explicitly trained for.

I should say we also ask a separate question about full automation of labor, which is when all occupations are fully automatable, and interestingly people tend to give much later dates for that even though it's conceptually pretty similar. That gap tells you something about how fragile these forecasts are. People's answers depend a lot on framing, which is one reason I'm cautious about treating any particular number as a precise prediction. But I do think the definition is still useful, because it's trying to point at the moment where humans stop being the main bottleneck on getting cognitive work done, and that seems like the thing that actually matters for what happens next.

r001.rationale: It defines the threshold as unaided machines accomplishing every task better than human workers.

r002.rationale: It says the capability could come from a collection of different systems rather than one monolithic system.

r003.rationale: It defines the threshold as unaided machines accomplishing every task more cheaply than human workers.

astra-6.text: I think of high-level machine intelligence as AI being able to do essentially all the tasks that humans can do, at least as well as humans and at a lower cost. That doesn’t necessarily mean a single system that can do everything. You could have a collection of different systems that, between them, cover all those tasks. So it’s more a claim about the capabilities available than about a particular architecture or how human-like the systems are.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can do essentially all human tasks “at least as well,” not better, and does not say they perform them unaided.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a collection of different systems could cover all the tasks, rather than one system doing everything.

r003.rationale: The response mentions lower cost, but does not state that machines perform every task unaided.

sol-6.1.text: I think of high-level machine intelligence as AI systems that can collectively do essentially all of the tasks that humans can do, at least as well as humans and at lower cost. That doesn’t necessarily mean one system that has every human capability. You could have different systems doing different things, and together they would meet that definition. So it’s more a claim about the range of work AI can perform than about whether we’ve built something that thinks like a person.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could perform essentially all human tasks at least as well as humans, but it does not say machines work unaided or perform every task better than humans.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says different AI systems could do different things and collectively meet the definition, rather than requiring one system with every capability.

r003.rationale: The response mentions lower cost, but does not say machines perform every task unaided and more cheaply than human workers.
